newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Cardoso toasts CVRD selloff in reform drive.
newsitem.headline: Cardoso toasts CVRD selloff in reform drive.

text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's government Wednesday toasted the biggest victory of his drive to reform the Brazilian economy: selling a controlling stake in mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce.

In a Rio de Janeiro Stock Exchange auction Tuesday, an international consortium, led by Brazilian steelmaker Companhia Siderurgica Nacional (CSN) and financed mainly by Charlotte, N.C.-based NationsBank Corp., agreed to pay 3.33 billion reais ($3.12 billion) for 41.7 percent of CVRD's voting stock.

The auction, to be followed by the sale of stock to CVRD employees and a global stock offering of the government's remaining 51 percent stake, kicked off the biggest privatisation in Latin American and could eventually put more than $5 billion in government coffers.

Planning Minister Antonio Kandir, the architect of the government privatisation programme, said he was delighted by the 20 percent premium paid over the base price, saying it was "above expectations."

Even as the government celebrated the completion of the auction, a slew of lawsuits that delayed the sell-off from its original April 29 date continued unabated. A judge in Rio de Janeiro issued an injunction she said suspended the outcome of the auction.

Government officials said they would appeal the latest injunction and promised to stand by any court decision suspending the sale. However, analysts said it was unlikely any new action could reverse the auction.
Tuesday's newspapers were quick to hail CSN President Benjamin Steinbruch, who was dubbed the new "Baron of Brazilian Steel."

Analysts said the CSN-led consortium -- which, in addition to NationsBank, was funded by Citibank of New York, financier George Soros and several Brazilian pension funds -- will directly or indirectly control up to 80 percent of Brazilian steel production.
Besides managing the world's single biggest iron ore mine, CVRD has a stake in all major Brazilian steelmakers, including CSN.
Asked if all this concentrated industrial power did not raise the threat of a monopoly, Steinbruch said he had no plans to build a vast steel and iron ore holding.
"We have no intention of building a steel holding. We believe in putting together a more flexible system," Steinbruch told reporters in a morning television news programme.
Steinbruch said he was confident the legal obstacles blocking the sale would soon be overcome and said CVRD's new management would not make any changes for at least six months.

The completion of the CVRD auction, after months of stiff opposition in Congress and intense legal wrangling, is a major political victory for President Cardoso, who has led a crusade to reduce government influence over the Brazilian economy.
Newspapers hailed the CVRD sale as a victory for free enterprise but urged Cardoso to press ahead with the rest of the privatisation programme.

"The government must redouble its efforts and show the same determination when the time comes to privatise the state power and telecommunications sectors," O Globo daily said in a front-page editorial.
